tasks.intent: Show me US real GDP growth forecasts for the next few years with the range of uncertainty around each year's estimate, not just the point forecast.

data.description: Survey of Professional Forecasters projections of US annual real GDP growth, giving a central estimate plus the 10th/25th/75th/90th percentile of forecaster views for each projection year.
data.shape: 1 series x ~5 forecast years, each with a central estimate and a symmetric-ish quantile band

expected.chart_family: line with a graduated confidence band (fan chart), central estimate as a line and nested percentile ranges as translucent bands of increasing lightness
expected.key_insight: The point forecast is modest and roughly flat, but the fan widens sharply with horizon: near-term growth is bounded tightly while the outer years admit outcomes from mild recession to boom, so the honest story is escalating uncertainty rather than a confident path.

failure_modes: Plotting only the central estimate as a single clean line and dropping the percentile bands entirely, presenting a false precision that hides the entire point of the request (Cairo: the graphic must show what the data does not know).

Drawing the uncertainty as discrete error-bar whiskers at each year rather than a continuous band, breaking the Gestalt continuity that lets the reader see uncertainty compounding smoothly across the horizon.

Rendering the nested percentile ranges in saturated rainbow fills instead of a single hue graded by lightness, so band color reads as an unordered categorical key when it actually encodes an ordered probability mass (color: lightness, not hue, carries the ordinal confidence level).
Truncating the y-axis to frame only the central estimates so the widening band is clipped at the panel edge, amputating the outer-percentile outcomes that are the message (Tufte lie factor).

Filling the outermost band as opaquely as the innermost so the visual weight is uniform, defeating the graded-lightness cue that should make the most-probable core read as denser than the tails (Ware: encode probability density with perceived opacity).

tasks.intent: Compare vaccine efficacy across a handful of COVID vaccines showing the efficacy estimate and its 95% confidence interval for each, so I can see which differences are actually distinguishable.

data.description: Reported phase-3 primary-endpoint efficacy against symptomatic disease for several authorized COVID-19 vaccines, each with a point estimate and a 95% confidence interval from the trial.
data.shape: ~7 vaccines x 1 quantitative estimate each, with a lower and upper CI bound

expected.chart_family: horizontal dot-and-whisker (interval) plot, one row per vaccine, sorted by point estimate, with confidence intervals drawn as whiskers
expected.key_insight: Vaccines with non-overlapping intervals are genuinely distinguishable while those whose intervals overlap heavily are not; ranking by point estimate alone would overstate small, statistically indistinguishable gaps, and wide intervals flag small or noisier trials.

failure_modes: Drawing efficacy as plain bars with no interval at all, forcing an area/length read of a point estimate and erasing the sampling uncertainty that determines whether any ranking is real (Cleveland & McGill; Cairo).

Leaving the vaccines in alphabetical or data-file order rather than sorting by point estimate, so the reader cannot perceive the ranking the intervals are meant to qualify (ordering principle for comparison).
Adding bars behind the dots that begin at a non-zero baseline, so bar length exaggerates efficacy differences while the whiskers quietly contradict the bar heights (Tufte lie factor).

Encoding each vaccine's whisker in a different saturated hue as if color carried meaning, when the vaccines are nominal and the only quantitative channels are position and interval length (color: no hue scale for nominal rows).

Using whisker caps and dots so visually heavy that overlapping intervals blur into one another, destroying the figure-ground separation needed to judge which intervals actually overlap (Ware; Gestalt).

tasks.intent: Plot the projected global mean surface temperature rise through 2100 under one emissions scenario, showing the model spread so readers see the range and not just the central projection.

data.description: CMIP/IPCC projected global surface temperature anomaly relative to pre-industrial for a single SSP scenario, given as a multi-model mean with a likely-range envelope (e.g. 5th-95th percentile) by year.
data.shape: 1 scenario x ~80 projection years, each with a central value and a likely-range band

expected.chart_family: line with a shaded uncertainty band (central projection plus a translucent likely-range envelope that widens over the century)
expected.key_insight: The central line rises steadily, but the model spread fans out with time so that by 2100 the likely range spans well over a degree; the responsible read is a band of plausible futures, and stating the scenario is essential because the band is conditional on it.

failure_modes: Showing only the multi-model mean line and omitting the envelope, implying a single deterministic future and hiding the inter-model spread that is the requested content (Cairo: do not present projection as certainty).

Overlaying several scenarios' bands in overlapping saturated fills so the envelopes muddy into an unreadable wash, when the ask is one scenario cleanly shown (Ware: overlapping translucency destroys the density cue).

Coloring the band with a red-to-blue diverging ramp keyed to temperature, implying a meaningful midpoint on the fill channel that carries no such value here, competing with the real position encoding (color).
Truncating the y-axis well above zero and stretching the panel so the central slope reads as a vertical cliff, inflating the apparent rate (Tufte lie factor).

Failing to label the scenario and the band's percentile definition, leaving the envelope's meaning ambiguous and the whole figure uninterpretable (Cairo; typography: quantitative annotations must be explicit).

tasks.intent: Show median household income by US state with the margin of error on each estimate, so I can see which state-to-state differences are real and which are within sampling noise.

data.description: American Community Survey 1-year median household income by state, each estimate published with a 90% margin of error.
data.shape: ~51 states x 1 quantitative estimate each, with a margin of error
data.identifier: B19013 (ACS median household income, with MOE)

expected.chart_family: horizontal dot-and-whisker (interval) plot, one row per state, sorted by estimate, with the margin of error drawn as a whisker
expected.key_insight: States near each other in the ranking have overlapping margins and are not reliably distinguishable, so the apparent fine-grained ordering is partly noise; only the gap between the top and bottom clusters is clearly real, and small states carry visibly wider intervals.

failure_modes: Rendering the estimates as a choropleth map with a single fill per state and no way to show the margin of error, which answers 'where' but cannot express uncertainty and lets large low-income states dominate the visual over small ones (chart-selection; Cairo).

Drawing bars from a non-zero baseline with no error whiskers, so tiny truncation-inflated gaps between adjacent states read as decisive when they are within the margin of error (Tufte lie factor; Cleveland & McGill).
Leaving states in alphabetical order rather than sorting by estimate, so the reader cannot see the ranking the margins are meant to qualify (ordering principle).
Binning income into a sequential rainbow palette whose perceived lightness is non-monotonic, so the color scale reads as a false ordinal ladder that fights the position encoding (color).
Making the whiskers too faint or too short relative to marker size to judge overlap, defeating the single purpose of plotting the margin of error (Ware; Gestalt figure-ground).

tasks.intent: Show OECD PISA average math scores for a set of countries with each country's confidence interval, so I can tell which countries are actually ahead of which rather than reading a spurious league table.

data.description: PISA mean mathematics score by country for the most recent cycle, each reported with a standard error from which a 95% confidence interval is derived.
data.shape: ~12 countries x 1 quantitative mean each, with a standard error / confidence interval

expected.chart_family: horizontal dot-and-whisker (interval) plot, countries sorted by mean score, confidence intervals shown as whiskers
expected.key_insight: Countries clustered within a few points share overlapping intervals and cannot be reliably rank-ordered, so the familiar PISA league table overstates precision; only clearly separated tiers of countries are genuinely distinguishable.

failure_modes: Presenting the scores as a ranked bar chart with no intervals, manufacturing a precise league table from means whose confidence intervals overlap and thereby endorsing distinctions the data cannot support (Cairo; the canonical PISA-ranking abuse).

Truncating the score axis to a narrow window around the means so a handful of indistinguishable points spread across the full panel width, visually magnifying differences that lie within the intervals (Tufte lie factor).
Sorting countries alphabetically instead of by score, so the tiers the intervals reveal cannot be read off the figure (ordering principle for comparison).

Assigning each country a distinct saturated hue as if color were informative, when the rows are nominal and only position and interval length carry meaning, adding chartjunk that competes with the data (color; Tufte).

Drawing overlapping whiskers at a weight and density that blur adjacent intervals together, so the reader cannot see which pairs actually overlap, defeating the comparison the chart exists to enable (Ware; Gestalt figure-ground).
